content: 1,3-Dichloropropane, a chemical found in drinking water, exhibits low acute toxicity. There is some evidence suggesting it may be genotoxic in bacterial systems. The current data are insufficient to establish a guideline value for its presence in drinking water. 1,3-Dichloropropene, a soil fumigant used to control soil pests like nematodes in sandy soils, is a mixture of cis and trans isomers. Tumors have also been observed in the bladder and lungs of female mice and the liver of male rats. Long-term inhalation studies in rats have been negative, but benign lung tumors have been reported in mice. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies 1,3-dichloropropene as a Group 2B carcinogen, meaning it is possibly carcinogenic to humans. Chlorophenoxy herbicides, including dichlorprop, degrade in the environment within several days. In rats, renal toxicity was observed at 64 mg/kg body weight per day in a two-year dietary study. Detection limits for these herbicides in water range from 1 µg/L to 1 mg/L, depending on the analytical method. IARC classifies chlorophenoxy herbicides as Group 2B carcinogens, but the available data do not allow for a definitive assessment of their carcinogenic potential in humans. Drinking water guidelines for these compounds are based on a threshold approach for other toxic effects, such as liver hypertrophy and kidney changes observed in animal studies. Dichlorvos, an organophosphorus insecticide, is used for household pest control and protecting stored products. It is highly mobile in soils but degrades rapidly through microbial activity and hydrolysis. Dichlorvos inhibits cholinesterase activity, causing neurotoxicity, but it is unlikely to be genotoxic in vivo or carcinogenic to humans. Some reproductive toxicity has been observed in rats, but it does not cause developmental toxicity or teratogenic effects. The compound is no longer approved in some jurisdictions due to concerns over its acute toxicity. Dicofol, an organochlorine acaricide derived from DDT, is used to control plant-eating mites. It is slightly water-soluble and binds strongly to soil, with limited data on its occurrence in water. Dicofol has been associated with liver tumors in male mice at high doses but is not genotoxic. Dicofol is being phased out in the USA and is no longer approved in the European Union. It has been proposed as a persistent organic pollutant under the Stockholm Convention. Di(2-ethylhexyl) adipate (DEHA) is primarily used as a plasticizer. At high dietary levels, it induces peroxisomal proliferation in rodent livers, which is associated with liver tumors. DEHA is not genotoxic and has been classified by IARC as Group 3, meaning it is not classifiable as to its carcinogenicity to humans. A health-based value of 80 µg/L can be calculated for DEHA in drinking water, but it typically occurs at concentrations well below levels of health concern. Di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP), another plasticizer, is primarily absorbed from food. It is widely distributed in the body, with the highest levels in the liver and adipose tissue, but does not accumulate significantly. DEHP causes hepatic peroxisome proliferation in rodents, but primates, including humans, are less sensitive to this effect. It has been classified by IARC as Group 2B, possibly carcinogenic to humans. Dimethoate, an organophosphorus insecticide, is used in agriculture and household pest control. It inhibits cholinesterase activity and is a skin irritant but is not carcinogenic in rodents. Although in vitro studies suggest mutagenic potential, this is not expressed in vivo. Dimethoate's reproductive toxicity in rats raises concerns, but no data are available to assess whether these effects are secondary to cholinesterase inhibition. Further evaluation of its toxicity may be needed. 1,4-Dioxane is used as a stabilizer and solvent in various industrial applications. It is not removed by conventional water treatment processes but can be effectively removed by biological activated carbon treatment. It has been shown to cause tumors in rodents, including hepatic and nasal cavity tumors, and is classified by IARC as Group 2B, possibly carcinogenic to humans. Evidence for human carcinogenicity is inadequate due to limited data. Diquat, a non-selective herbicide, is highly water-soluble but strongly adsorbed to soil. It is not carcinogenic in mice or rats and does not cause reproductive or developmental toxicity. Diquat concentrations in water should be kept as low as possible. Endosulfan, an insecticide used worldwide, is not widely found in the aquatic environment but has been detected in agricultural runoff and industrialized areas. It is not genotoxic or carcinogenic in long-term studies. The kidney is the primary target organ for toxicity. Endosulfan may bind to estrogen receptors and disrupt the endocrine system. It occurs in drinking water at concentrations well below levels of health concern. Endrin, a broad-spectrum insecticide and rodenticide, is now rarely used. It is listed under the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants. The primary site of action is the central nervous system. Toxicological data are insufficient to determine its carcinogenic potential in humans. Epichlorohydrin, used in the manufacture of resins and water treatment polymers, is a genotoxic carcinogen. It is not removed by conventional water treatment processes, and its concentrations in drinking water are controlled by limiting its content in treatment chemicals. The guideline value for epichlorohydrin is provisional due to uncertainties surrounding its toxicity.
